Faculty
Geology prepares you to step into the role of the next generation of Earth scientists through rigorous field- and lab-based training and hands-on research spanning energy and petroleum systems, hydrogeology and water resources, geophysics and earthquakes, geochemistry, and Earth structure and dynamics. These provide the scientific foundation for addressing global challenges such as climate change, natural disasters, and sustainable resource management. As part of Oklahoma State University’s land-grant mission, we partner with industry, government, and communities to deliver interdisciplinary science and workforce-ready leaders whose work expands the frontiers of geoscience and produces tangible societal benefit. By training critical thinkers who connect science with real-world solutions, geology programs help ensure the planet’s safety, sustainability, and resilience for future generations. We advance solutions that matter for Oklahoma and for our planet—responsible stewardship of our abundant energy and mineral resources, protection and sustainable management of our groundwater and surface water, and improved understanding and mitigation of geologic hazards. The Boone Pickens School of Geology maintains three undergraduate degree programs, (1) Geology, (2) Environmental Geoscience, and (3) Geophysics. We offer research opportunities in cutting-edge facilities, scholarships to support student success, and opportunities to develop a career that matches your passion and curiosity.
Geology
Geology is the study of Earth, its materials, history, and the dynamic processes that continue to shape the planet we live on. By examining rocks, minerals, fossils, and landforms, geologists reconstruct Earth’s past and use that knowledge to better understand the forces driving earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building, and landscape change. These insights also help scientists anticipate future environmental and geologic events that affect people and societies.
Geologists play a vital role in addressing some of the world’s most pressing challenges. They explore for energy and mineral resources, study and protect groundwater systems, assess natural hazards such as landslides and earthquakes, and help manage the land and water resources that sustain us and our communities. Because many geological processes occur at or near Earth’s surface, geoscientists often work in the field, combining outdoor investigation with laboratory analysis and advanced analytical technologies.
Within geology, students can pursue a wide range of specialized interests. Areas such as petroleum geology, hydrogeology (groundwater science), geomorphology (the study of landscapes and surface processes), structural geology (the deformation of Earth’s crust), and paleontology (the study of fossils and the history of life) allow geoscientists to focus on the aspects of Earth science that most inspire them. A degree in geology provides a strong scientific foundation and prepares students for careers in energy, environmental consulting, water resources, natural hazard assessment, research, and many other fields where understanding Earth systems is essential.
Environmental Geoscience
Environmental Geoscience examines the complex interactions between humans and the natural Earth system. It focuses on how human activities influence the land, water, and atmosphere—and how natural processes such as climate variability, groundwater movement, erosion, and natural hazards shape the environments in which societies live and develop. By understanding these interactions, environmental geoscientists work to diagnose environmental problems and develop science-based solutions.
Environmental geoscientists investigate issues such as groundwater contamination, water resource sustainability, soil and ecosystem health, environmental pollution, and the impacts of natural hazards. In many ways, they function like physicians for the Earth system—using scientific tools and data to assess environmental conditions, identify the causes of problems, and recommend strategies for restoration, protection, and sustainable management.
Students in the Environmental Geoscience program earn an interdisciplinary STEM degree that integrates geology, hydrology, chemistry, and environmental science. Through fieldwork, laboratory analysis, and data-driven problem solving, students develop the skills needed to address real-world environmental challenges. Graduates are prepared for careers in environmental consulting, water resources management, environmental protection, and public policy, as well as for advanced study in environmental and Earth sciences.
Geophysics
Geophysics is the study of the Earth and other planets using the principles of physics, mathematics, and advanced computational methods to investigate processes that cannot be observed directly. By applying technologies such as seismic imaging, gravity and magnetic measurements, electrical methods, and remote sensing, geophysicists explore the structure and dynamics of the Earth from the near surface to deep within the planet.
Geophysicists play a central role in discovering and managing Earth’s resources, including energy, minerals, and groundwater. They also use geophysical tools to detect earthquakes, map subsurface structures, locate subsurface resources and buried hazards, and identify environmental contamination. These approaches allow scientists to better understand natural systems while supporting responsible resource development and environmental stewardship.
The Bachelor of Science in Geophysics provides students with rigorous training that integrates geology, physics, mathematics, and computer modelling. Through coursework, field investigations, and hands-on experience with modern geophysical instrumentation and data analysis, students develop strong analytical and quantitative skills. Graduates are well prepared for advanced study in geophysics and related Earth sciences, as well as for careers in the energy, environmental, engineering, and regulatory sectors where geophysical expertise is increasingly in demand.
Research, Scholarships, and Careers
Students majoring in Geology, Environmental Geoscience, or Geophysics receive a rigorous, hands-on education designed to prepare them for leadership roles in the Earth and environmental sciences. Our programs combine strong scientific foundations with field experience, laboratory research, and modern analytical technologies, giving students the skills needed to pursue rewarding careers or continue to graduate study.
The Boone Pickens School of Geology offers multiple pathways for advanced training, including an Accelerated M.S. program, Master of Science (M.S.), and Ph.D. degrees. Both undergraduate and graduate students have opportunities to work alongside faculty on cutting-edge research and to participate in community and campus outreach activities that connect geoscience with real-world challenges.
Faculty research spans a wide range of topics that address critical questions about Earth systems and resources. These include plate tectonics, conventional and unconventional energy resources, environmental and engineering geoscience, carbon sequestration, paleoclimatology, and satellite remote sensing. Students benefit from working in a research environment supported by expert faculty, advanced laboratories, modern technologies, and an active culture of scientific discovery.
The school also provides departmental scholarships for full-time undergraduate majors based on academic achievement and financial need. Graduate students may be supported through teaching assistantships, research assistantships, and fellowships, allowing them to gain professional experience while pursuing advanced degrees.
Graduates of our programs enter a wide range of careers in both applied and research-focused fields. Geoscientists work in energy and mineral exploration, groundwater and water resource management, environmental consulting, hazard assessment, and environmental protection. Career paths are available with private industry, government agencies, national laboratories, consulting firms, and universities, as well as in education at the secondary and university levels.
A career in the geosciences can take you from field investigations using advanced instrumentation to laboratory-based research and global scientific collaboration. Whether working to understand Earth’s history, develop sustainable energy and water resources, or address environmental challenges, students in the Boone Pickens School of Geology turn curiosity about the planet into meaningful careers that help shape a more sustainable future.

Prerequisites
The student should have at least 30 credit hours in geosciences. Credit hours must include courses in physical geology, historical geology, rocks and minerals/mineralogy, sedimentology/stratigraphy, structural geology, field camp, or other courses relevant to the student's graduate research. Additional undergraduate requirements to enter the graduate programs include: two courses in chemistry/geochemistry, two courses in physics, and/or math courses through calculus II. Deficiencies in coursework must be made up by the student after entering the program. The Graduate Record Examination is recommended, but not required, for admission to the program.
The Master of Science Degree
The MS is awarded through the completion of a thesis. Each candidate must complete at least 30 semester credit hours of work beyond the prerequisites. As many as 12 of these may be taken in other departments of the University upon approval by the candidate's advisory committee. A final defense of the thesis and the research that it documents is required of all students.
The Doctor of Philosophy Degree
The PhD is awarded upon completion of a doctoral dissertation. A minimum of 60 credit hours (coursework and research hours) beyond the MS or MA degree are required for the PhD. Under normal circumstances, students must hold a master's degree in geology or a related field to be accepted into the PhD program. However, under exceptional circumstances, students may be accepted directly into the PhD program without a master's degree. Such students will be required to complete a total of 90 semester credit hours (coursework and research hours) to earn their degree. Such decisions are made by the entire faculty of the School of Geology, upon recommendation of the Graduate Advisor. To be admitted to candidacy, students must pass a written and oral qualifying exam, and successfully defend their dissertation research proposal and pass an associated comprehensive exam. The PhD is conferred after the successful defense of the dissertation.
Accelerated Master of Science Degree
Our School is proud to offer an Accelerated MS option. Students who wish to pursue an Accelerated Master's should have completed 90 or more hours toward their BS by the end of their term of application, including GEOL 3014 and GEOL 3034, and should have a strong background with undergraduate research. Students who are admitted into the Accelerated Master's program will be eligible to share 9 credit hours between their BS and MS degrees.
